title: Asteroids
description: Asteroids, Atari's 1979 vector classic, puts the player in a lone ship drifting through an asteroid field rendered in glowing lines. Thrust rotates and pushes the ship with real momentum, so stopping takes as long as starting, and every large rock splits into smaller, faster fragments when shot. The saucer that occasionally crosses the screen adds a moving threat to the drifting rocks.
body:
Asteroids, Atari's 1979 vector classic, puts the player in a lone ship drifting through an asteroid field rendered in glowing lines. Thrust rotates and pushes the ship with real momentum, so stopping takes as long as starting, and every large rock splits into smaller, faster fragments when shot. The saucer that occasionally crosses the screen adds a moving threat to the drifting rocks.

The tribute demo is an original vector-style miniature: a ship starts at [4, 5] among 4 drifting rocks on a glowing grid, thrusting with momentum, turning, and firing at rocks that split when hit. It captures the feel of the arcade original's line-drawn space without copying its code, art, or sound.

Momentum is the whole skill: a player who thrusts in short taps keeps the ship controllable, while long burns send it sliding across the field. Clearing large rocks near the edges first keeps the center open, and the hyperspace jump is a last resort, since it can drop the ship onto a rock.
controls: Type thrust/left/right/shoot to fly and fire, quit to stop.

body:
Asteroids Deluxe, Atari's 1981 follow-up, keeps the drifting ship and splitting rocks but adds new hazards: a shield that protects the ship briefly, and killer satellites that break apart into hunter drones. The graphics are sharper, the rocks are more varied, and the pace is noticeably faster than the original.

The shield changes the risk calculus, letting a player survive a collision that would have ended a run in the original. Killer satellites should be broken at range, since their hunter drones are far more dangerous up close than the satellite itself.

title: Battlezone
description: Battlezone, Atari's 1980 vector tank game, is one of the first first-person arcade experiences. The player drives a tank across a wireframe plain, viewed through a periscope-style cabinet, and duels enemy tanks, missiles, and flying saucers that appear on the horizon. Its stark green lines and radar display made it feel like a genuine combat simulator.
body:
Battlezone, Atari's 1980 vector tank game, is one of the first first-person arcade experiences. The player drives a tank across a wireframe plain, viewed through a periscope-style cabinet, and duels enemy tanks, missiles, and flying saucers that appear on the horizon. Its stark green lines and radar display made it feel like a genuine combat simulator.

The tribute demo is an original vector-style miniature: a ship starts at [6, 7] among 6 drifting rocks on a glowing grid, thrusting with momentum, turning, and firing at rocks that split when hit. It captures the feel of the arcade original's line-drawn space without copying its code, art, or sound.

The radar is as important as the viewport: enemies appear on radar before they are visible, so a good driver turns toward the blip early. Long-range shots work, but the enemy tanks dodge, so the winning habit is to fire, reposition, and fire again rather than trading shots head-on.

Its color vector display and escalating tube shapes were unlike anything else on the floor.

Thrust burns precious fuel, gravity pulls constantly, and a landing that is too fast or too tilted ends in a crash. It is a quiet, precise game of physics rather than a shooter, and one of the earliest arcade simulations.

Lunar Lander, Atari's 1979 vector simulation, asks the player to land a module gently on the moon's surface. Thrust burns precious fuel, gravity pulls constantly, and a landing that is too fast or too tilted ends in a crash. It is a quiet, precise game of physics rather than a shooter, and one of the earliest arcade simulations.

It captures the feel of the arcade original's line-drawn space without copying its code, art, or sound.

Fuel is the budget and descent speed is the danger: short, early burns cost less than a desperate late burn. A good landing starts high and slow, with the module already level before the final approach, rather than correcting at the last second.

The player's ship fires and thrusts with momentum, and the walls reflect both ships and shots, so every missed shot can come back around. It captures the feel of the arcade original's line-drawn space without copying its code, art, or sound.

Bouncing walls make the arena a geometry puzzle: a shot fired down a long diagonal can hit an enemy two reflections later. The safest position is near a corner with an escape route, since enemies bounce unpredictably through the center.

title: Quantum
description: Quantum, Atari's 1982 vector game, drops the shooting entirely: the player pilots a probe that captures atomic particles by circling them with a capture tail. Enclosing a particle without touching it scores points, and larger particles need larger loops. It is a rare arcade game about drawing shapes rather than firing weapons.
body:
Quantum, Atari's 1982 vector game, drops the shooting entirely: the player pilots a probe that captures atomic particles by circling them with a capture tail. Enclosing a particle without touching it scores points, and larger particles need larger loops. It is a rare arcade game about drawing shapes rather than firing weapons.

The tribute demo is an original vector-style miniature: a ship starts at [8, 5] among 6 drifting rocks on a glowing grid, thrusting with momentum, turning, and firing at rocks that split when hit. It captures the feel of the arcade original's line-drawn space without copying its code, art, or sound.

Capture loops must close without touching the particle, so the skill is in judging the loop's size before committing. Small loops are safe but score little, while a big loop around a cluster risks brushing a second particle mid-draw.

title: Gravitar
description: Gravitar, Atari's 1982 vector game, is one of the hardest arcade games ever made. The player pilots a ship with real gravity and momentum through a solar system, landing on planets to destroy reactor bunkers while fighting gravity, fuel limits, and turrets. Each planet has its own gravity and terrain.
body:
Gravitar, Atari's 1982 vector game, is one of the hardest arcade games ever made. The player pilots a ship with real gravity and momentum through a solar system, landing on planets to destroy reactor bunkers while fighting gravity, fuel limits, and turrets. Each planet has its own gravity and terrain.

The tribute demo is an original vector-style miniature: a ship starts at [5, 8] among 5 drifting rocks on a glowing grid, thrusting with momentum, turning, and firing at rocks that split when hit. It captures the feel of the arcade original's line-drawn space without copying its code, art, or sound.

Gravity is the opponent on every planet: thrust must counteract the pull constantly, and a ship that stops thrusting falls. Learning one planet's gravity at a time, starting with the gentlest, builds the feel needed for the harsher worlds.
controls: Type thrust/left/right/shoot to fly and fire, quit to stop.

title: Star Castle
description: Star Castle, Cinematronics' 1980 vector game, centers on a rotating cannon protected by three concentric rings. The player must blast through the rings to hit the cannon, while the cannon fires back and mines drift across the screen. The rings regenerate, so the attack must be pressed before the defense rebuilds.
body:
Star Castle, Cinematronics' 1980 vector game, centers on a rotating cannon protected by three concentric rings. The player must blast through the rings to hit the cannon, while the cannon fires back and mines drift across the screen. The rings regenerate, so the attack must be pressed before the defense rebuilds.

The tribute demo is an original vector-style miniature: a ship starts at [6, 9] among 6 drifting rocks on a glowing grid, thrusting with momentum, turning, and firing at rocks that split when hit. It captures the feel of the arcade original's line-drawn space without copying its code, art, or sound.

Ring-breaking is a timing problem: the rings rotate, so the gap moves, and the cannon fires whenever the player lingers. The best runs break one ring, retreat to dodge the cannon's return fire, and return through the same gap before it closes.
controls: Type thrust/left/right/shoot to fly and fire, quit to stop.

title: Tail Gunner
description: Tail Gunner, Cinematronics' 1979 vector game, puts the player in the rear gunner seat of a spaceship, shooting at pursuing enemy fighters. The view looks backward down the ship's tail, and enemy ships sweep in from the edges of the screen. It is one of the earliest first-person perspective shooters in the arcade.
body:
Tail Gunner, Cinematronics' 1979 vector game, puts the player in the rear gunner seat of a spaceship, shooting at pursuing enemy fighters. The view looks backward down the ship's tail, and enemy ships sweep in from the edges of the screen. It is one of the earliest first-person perspective shooters in the arcade.

The tribute demo is an original vector-style miniature: a ship starts at [7, 5] among 7 drifting rocks on a glowing grid, thrusting with momentum, turning, and firing at rocks that split when hit. It captures the feel of the arcade original's line-drawn space without copying its code, art, or sound.

Pursuers sweep in arcs, so the gunner must lead targets that cross the screen diagonally rather than aiming at where they are. Short bursts conserve the gun's fire rate for the next wave, which arrives faster than the last.
controls: Type thrust/left/right/shoot to fly and fire, quit to stop.
